pr_title: Fix an issue that a Pod's nominatedNodeName cannot be cleared upon node deletion
pr_body:
**What type of PR is this?**

/kind bug
/sig scheduling

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

This PR tries to fix an issue that a Pod's nominatedNodeName cannot be cleared upon node deletion. Detailed reproducing steps please check #85677 and the integration test of this PR.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:

Fixes #85677

**Special notes for your reviewer**:

A side effect is that upon unexpected internal errors during preemption, the nominatedNode would be returned as "", so the pod's non-nil nominatedNodeName will be cleared. It means its reserved room on a node can be occupied by other pods before it's scheduled next time.
But compared to the issue that its nominatedNode is unable to be cleared, the impact is negligible.

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**:

```release-note
Fixed an issue that a Pod's nominatedNodeName cannot be cleared upon node deletion.
```

issue_context.title: Scheduler does not clear nominatedNodeName on Pod when node is no longer valid
issue_context.body:
**What happened**:

Scheduler decided that it wants to schedule Pod P on Node N after preempting some pods from N.
It set the P.nominatedNodeName to N. After a while (before scheduling actually happened) node N was removed from the cluster.
Scheduler did not reset P.nominatedNodeName to empty value.

**What you expected to happen**:

I would expect scheduler to unset P.nominatedNodeName when the node is no longer valid.
The trivial reason for node not being valid any more is it is removed from the cluster. 
But there are more cases to cover. Out of the top of my head I may think of:
- extra Pod was scheduled to node and there is not enough resources any more
  - either scheduled by scheduler
  - or directly as static pod/daemonset
- node became unschedulable

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

We did not try to reproduce issue manually. Yet following setup should work.
- create cluster with nodes A and B.
- ensure all system pods are running on A. Fill up A so it does not have spare resources.
- add a low priority Pod L with long termination, with requests matching allocatable of B. It should be scheduled to B.
- add a high priority Pod H. It should get B as nominatedNodeName
- kill node B
- the H.nominatedNodeName will still point to B which is no longer in the cluster

**Anything else we need to know?**:

Current behavior does not play well with Cluster Autoscaler which assumes that Pod with nominatedNodeName will be scheduled in a while.
Therefore such pods do not trigger scale-up. If we can have P.nominatedNodeName set incorrectly for unbounded period of time CA will never
provision node for P to run.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):

We observed the behavior during presubmit tests which run k8s built from HEAD of master on 27.11.2019.

Versions logged in test log:
I1125 18:55:11.691] Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"18+", GitVersion:"v1.18.0-alpha.0.1183+414202578ba1ad", GitCommit:"414202578ba1ad53a26bc5126b3828a3a410097e", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2019-11-25T17:04:18Z", GoVersion:"go1.13.4", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
I1125 18:55:11.692] Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"18+", GitVersion:"v1.18.0-alpha.0.1183+414202578ba1ad", GitCommit:"414202578ba1ad53a26bc5126b3828a3a410097e", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2019-11-25T17:04:18Z", GoVersion:"go1.13.4", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}

- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
GCE

/sig scheduling
comments: /assign @ahg-g
/cc @MaciekPytel

Another interesting case would be creating a new pod with pod antiaffinity blocking the pod with nominated node name from scheduling:
1. Fill up a cluster with pods, including a long-terminating low-priority pod A. 
2. Create high-priority pod B that has the same requests as A.
3. Create pod C with negligible resource requests and zonal topology pod antiaffinity matching pod B (and no other pods in the cluster).

What I'd expect:
- Pod C keeps pending, nominatedNodeName is cleared.
- Pod A is restarted on the same node it was running before.

I haven't actually tested this scenario, so I'm not sure what will actually happen. If @losipiuk's report is correct, this may be a more convenient way of reproducing the issue (no need to add / remove nodes, it's not important which pod will go to which node).

@losipiuk  I'm not sure if we need to clear nominatedNodeName on Pod when node is no longer valid immediately.  And we have other logic to clear nominatedNodeName. 

-------
Reuse your example.
- create cluster with nodes A and B.
- ensure all system pods are running on A. Fill up A so it does not have spare resources.
- add a low priority Pod L with long termination, with requests matching allocatable of B. It should be scheduled to B.
- add a high priority Pod H. It should get B as nominatedNodeName
- kill node B
- the H.nominatedNodeName will still point to B which is no longer in the cluster
-------
After this, 
1.  The H will be scheduled again. Obviously it's going to fail.
2. The H will enter the preemption process and the `potentialNodes` is empty.  It will return itself as `nominatedPodsToClear`
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9474154012eedc547e1cfa58c4a8d5d0e3308290/pkg/scheduler/core/generic_scheduler.go#L342-L347
3. The preemption process will clean nominatedNodeName on the Pod H.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9474154012eedc547e1cfa58c4a8d5d0e3308290/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L489-L500

@denkensk when I have some time I will check if reproduction steps I describe actually work. But we surely observed pods with lingering nominatedNodeName which pointed to inexistent node, during our E2E tests.

Quick thought. The `Preempt()` method https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9474154012eedc547e1cfa58c4a8d5d0e3308290/pkg/scheduler/core/generic_scheduler.go#L328
has many return points. 
If it returned at the place you linked it seems `nominatedNodePool` should be cleared. 
But there are many return points below, which set the list of pods to be cleared to nil. 
Is it possible that for a pod to consistently exit from `Preempt` with one of those return points?

@losipiuk  I think you are right.  Actually there are many return points to return nil.  I think maybe we need to clear the `nominatedNode` of the pod after the filter failed again and before the new preemption process to avoid potential risks.  WDYT? @ahg-g

I believe it's a bug as in old logic, e.g., v1.18.3, if the Pod (with nominatedNodeName set) cannot be scheduled and also preemption doesn't help (@denkensk nil potentialNodes is a corner case, it's more common the pod can't fit on all potentialNodes), it won't hit L413:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2e7996e3e2712684bc73f0dec0200d64eec7fe40/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L404-L413 

then in old recordingFailure logic, nominatedNodeName remains as is.

In the latest codebase, @ahg-g introduced a fix to combine setting nominatedNodeName as well update the pod's unschedulable condition. However, this doesn't help in this issue either as it ignores the case when the pod's nominatedNodeName is nil:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c18bc7e9f7a27d7d197053d98c52896e1dc3bb3e/pkg/scheduler/scheduler.go#L389-L396

/reopen
as #91750 regresses - we need to come up with a complete fix.

Without this, this test would fail at the cleanup step: `defer cleanupPodsInNamespace(cs, t, testCtx.NS.Name)`.

This puzzled me as well, and here is my investigation. In the new test, it deleted a node, and then cleaned up all the Pods using `DeleteCollection`. However, one of the pods was placed on the deleted node. I think the **immediate** Pods deletion action resulted in the failure.

I tried to use curl to simulate this case. You can notice that pod2 keeps in terminating state instead of being deleted: 

```
root@wei-dev:~/manifests/certs# k get po -o wide
NAME   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP                NODE    NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES
pod1   1/1     Running   0          46s   192.168.192.168   node1   <none>           <none>
pod2   1/1     Running   0          3s    192.168.192.168   node2   <none>           <none>

root@wei-dev:~/manifests# k delete no node2
node "node2" deleted

root@wei-dev:~/manifests/certs# curl --key key --cert cert --cacert cacert -X DELETE https://localhost:6443/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods

root@wei-dev:~/manifests/certs# k get pod -o wide
NAME   READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE   IP                NODE    NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES
pod2   1/1     Terminating   0          56s   192.168.192.168   node2   <none>           <none>

# After 30 seconds
root@wei-dev:~/manifests/certs# k get pod -o wide
No resources found in default namespace.
# But in an integration test, I guess the Pod will be kept there, that's why the test would fail without enforcing a 0 termination grace period
```

---

I'm not sure it's a bug in `DeleteCollection` or as expected, but as setting it to an explicit 0 grace period won't result in any side effect, I think we can just merge it as is, WDYT?
This test can be merged with existing `TestNominatedNodeCleanUp` using table-test style.
